title: Binary Tree Maximum Path Sum
description: Post-order DFS. Each node returns the best single-branch gain (clamped at 0); a global tracks the best left+node+right path seen at any node.

conversation.intro: How an interview about this problem would actually play out. Each section has two parts: what you'd actually say out loud, and why that move matters. Tap a section to expand.

sections.title: 1. Restate & clarify
sections.prompt: Before touching code — pin down the inputs.
sections.say:
"So I need to find the maximum sum of any path in a binary tree, where a 'path' is a sequence of connected nodes via parent-child edges, and the path can start and end at any nodes — it doesn't need to go through the root, doesn't need to start or end at a leaf."

Then a few quick clarifying questions:
• Can values be negative? (Yes is the standard — that's what makes the problem interesting.)
• Does a path have to contain at least one node? (Yes — empty paths aren't counted, and a single node by itself is a valid path with sum = node.val.)
• Can a path go 'up and over' a node — i.e. left child → node → right child? (Yes, that's the through-path case, and it's the whole trick of the problem.)
• Just return the sum, not the path itself?
sections.why: The 'up and over' question is THE problem-defining clarification. If paths were strictly downward (root-to-leaf style), this would be a simple post-order recursion. But because paths can turn at any node — go up from left child, through the node, down to right child — there's a fundamental tension between 'best path through this node' (uses both children) and 'best path you can extend UPWARD from this node' (uses only one child, because a path can't fork). Forcing the interviewer to confirm the up-and-over case ensures you're solving the right problem.

sections.title: 2. Brute force first (out loud)
sections.prompt: Name the O(n²) DFS-from-every-node, then justify the O(n) post-order with two values.
sections.say:
"The brute force: for every node, do a DFS treating it as the 'apex' of the path. From the apex, walk down both children collecting the maximum-sum path on each side, sum those plus the apex value, that's the best path with this apex. Repeat for every node. That's O(n) per node times n nodes = O(n²).

The better approach: do ONE post-order traversal, and at each node compute two things:
(a) Best path THROUGH this node — uses left, node, right — this updates a global `best`.
(b) Best CHAIN ending at this node and extendable upward — can use only ONE side, because a path can't fork. This is what we RETURN to the parent.

The key trick: clamp each child's returned chain at 0. A negative-sum branch is worse than not including that branch at all, so we just skip it. Visit each node once → O(n)."
sections.why: The 'two values per node' framing is the load-bearing distinction that this problem rewards. Calling it out explicitly — 'through-path uses both children, return-chain uses one' — is what separates a derivation from a magic algorithm. The clamp-at-zero rule is the subtle bit that handles negative values cleanly; verbalizing why (negative is worse than nothing) shows you understand the decision rather than just writing `Math.max(gain, 0)`.

sections.title: 3. Spot the pattern
sections.prompt: What signal in the problem points to this two-values-per-node post-order shape?
sections.say:
"There are two markers that point to this specific shape. First, the answer depends on values aggregated bottom-up — each node's contribution depends on what its children contributed. That's post-order DFS. Second, and more importantly, there are TWO DIFFERENT THINGS we care about at each node: the answer we'd RECORD (best path through this node) versus the answer we'd RETURN (best chain ending here, extendable by the parent). These are different because a path can have AT MOST one 'turn' — once it goes up through a node and down the other child, it's closed. The parent can only extend a chain, never a turned path.

That 'record one thing, return another' shape — combined with closure-scoped state for the global best — is the technique. Whenever a tree problem has both 'global best across all subtrees' AND 'something I need to pass up to the parent,' this template applies. Same shape as Diameter of Binary Tree (LeetCode 543), where you return depth but record diameter."
sections.why: Naming the 'record one thing, return another' shape — and explicitly distinguishing the two values per node — is the derivation. Most candidates write the algorithm correctly but can't articulate why the two values are different. The connection to Diameter of Binary Tree (which has the same shape: return depth, update global diameter via left + right + 1) proves you see the template, not just this problem.

sections.title: 4. Trace through examples
sections.prompt: Walk a few inputs to confirm the model before writing the loop.
sections.intro: "Let me trace through a couple of cases to make sure my model is right." Three inputs cover the interesting behaviors — a tree where the answer doesn't touch the root, a single all-negative node, and a tiny tree where the answer goes THROUGH the root.

examples.note: Best path is 15→20→7 (sum 42), entirely in the right subtree — root -10 is NOT on the answer path.
examples.trace:
best = -Infinity
gain(9): no children. through = 9 + 0 + 0 = 9; best=9. return 9 + max(0,0) = 9.
gain(15): no children. through = 15; best=15. return 15.
gain(7):  no children. through = 7;  best still 15. return 7.
gain(20): left=max(15,0)=15, right=max(7,0)=7. through = 20+15+7 = 42; best=42. return 20+max(15,7) = 35.
gain(-10): left=max(9,0)=9, right=max(35,0)=35. through = -10+9+35 = 34; best still 42. return -10+max(9,35) = 25.
return 42

examples.note: Single all-negative node — defends `best = -Infinity` initial value, not 0.
examples.trace:
best = -Infinity
gain(-3): no children. through = -3 + 0 + 0 = -3; best = max(-Infinity, -3) = -3. return -3 + max(0,0) = -3.
return -3

examples.note: Tiny tree — answer is the through-path at root: 2 + 1 + 3 = 6.
examples.trace:
best = -Infinity
gain(2): through = 2; best=2. return 2.
gain(3): through = 3; best=3. return 3.
gain(1): left=max(2,0)=2, right=max(3,0)=3. through = 1+2+3 = 6; best=6. return 1+max(2,3) = 4.
return 6

sections.why: The first trace makes the through-vs-return distinction visible: at node 20, the through-path candidate is 42 (uses both children), but what we return upward is 35 (uses only one child — the path can't fork). At node -10 we'd return 25 upward, but the global `best` stays at 42. The all-negative trace defends the `best = -Infinity` initialization — if we'd started best at 0, we'd incorrectly return 0 for the tree `[-3]`. These two bugs are the most common in this problem; the traces expose them.

sections.title: 5. Edge cases to mention
sections.prompt: What inputs would trip up a careless implementation?
sections.say:
"Before I declare it done, let me think about edges:
• Single node, positive → best = node.val. ✓
• Single node, negative → best = node.val (must be negative). This is why `best` starts at `-Infinity`, not 0. If you initialize to 0, you'd return 0 on `[-3]` which is wrong.
• All-negative tree → answer is the largest single value (best single node). The clamp-at-zero ensures children contribute 0 instead of their negative sum, so each node's through-path is just node.val. Best across all nodes is max(all values).
• Tree where the answer doesn't go through root → handled because we update `best` at every node, not just the root.
• Left-skewed (degenerate to linked list) → recursion depth = n; same stack-overflow concern as any tree recursion.
• All-zero values → answer is 0. Initialization at -Infinity gets overridden by the first node's through-path.
• Very deep tree → recursion-stack risk, would need iterative post-order DFS as a fallback.
• Two equally-good paths → returns either's sum, problem only asks for the max not the path itself."
sections.why: The `-Infinity` vs 0 initialization is THE classic bug here, and naming it explicitly — with the `[-3]` counter-example that breaks the 0-init version — is the senior signal. The all-negative tree's reduction to 'best single value' is a nice corollary that proves the clamp-at-zero handles it cleanly; verbalizing that reduction shows you traced through the logic, not just memorized the algorithm.

sections.title: 6. Complexity & wrap-up
sections.prompt: How would you defend the complexity claim?
sections.say:
"Time is O(n) — each node is visited exactly once in post-order. The work per node is constant: two max calls, one addition, one comparison against global best, one return. No re-traversal, no memoization needed because the recursion tree mirrors the actual tree.

Space is O(h) for the recursion stack — log n balanced, n worst case skewed. The closure-scoped `best` is O(1).

The trick — return one value, update another — generalizes to a whole family of tree problems. Diameter of Binary Tree (LeetCode 543): return depth, update global diameter via `left_depth + right_depth`. Longest Univalue Path (LeetCode 687): return univalue chain length, update global with sum of both children. Same shape: post-order, two values per node, one extends upward and one is recorded globally.

If interview pushback questioned the O(h) stack on huge trees, I'd convert to iterative post-order with an explicit stack — same logic, just managing the stack frames manually. More code, same complexity."
sections.why: Naming the family — Diameter, Longest Univalue Path — proves you see this as a parameterized template, not a one-off. The 'return one, record another' shape is the abstract pattern, and showing you can apply it across problems is what distinguishes pattern recognition from memorization. The iterative-post-order fallback is the right answer to the stack-safety pushback.

walkthrough.intro: Step through the post-order DFS. At every node the trace shows (a) the upward gain returned to its parent — one branch only, clamped at 0 — and (b) the through-node path candidate (node.val + left + right) compared against the global best.

const root = { val: arr[0], left: null, right: null };
if (i < arr.length && arr[i] != null) { node.left = { val: arr[i], left: null, right: null }; q.push(node.left); }
if (i < arr.length && arr[i] != null) { node.right = { val: arr[i], left: null, right: null }; q.push(node.right); }
yield { line: 1, label: `enter maxPathSum — tree ${JSON.stringify(input)}`, state: { treeShape: input } };
yield { line: 2, label: 'init best = -Infinity', state: { treeShape: input, best: '-Infinity' } };

yield { line: 3, label: `call gain(${node.val}) — descend to children first`, state: { treeShape: input, current: node.val, best: best === -Infinity ? '-Infinity' : best, stackDepth: stack.length } };

yield { line: 5, label: `node ${node.val}: leftGain=max(${leftRaw},0)=${left}, rightGain=max(${rightRaw},0)=${right}`, state: { treeShape: input, current: node.val, leftRaw, rightRaw, left, right } };
yield { line: 7, label: `through-path candidate = ${node.val}+${left}+${right} = ${through}; best → ${best}`, state: { treeShape: input, current: node.val, through, best } };
yield { line: 8, label: `return upward gain ${node.val}+max(${left},${right}) = ${upward}`, state: { treeShape: input, current: node.val, upward, best } };
yield { line: 11, label: `done — return best = ${best}`, state: { treeShape: input, returns: best } };

notes: Distinguish two things at each node: (a) the best path through it using BOTH children — only updates `best`, never returned; (b) the upward gain via ONE child — what you return to the parent.
Clamp each child gain at 0: a negative branch is better skipped than taken.
`best` must start at `-Infinity`, not 0 — paths can be entirely negative (e.g. tree [-3]).

questions.q: Why is each child's gain clamped at 0 with `Math.max(gain, 0)`?
options: Because a negative-sum branch is worse than not taking that branch at all

questions.q: What does the recursive function RETURN to its caller?
options: The best path through the current node using both children
The best single-branch upward gain from this node (node.val + max(left, right))
The sum of every node in the subtree
questions.explain: The caller can only extend the path via ONE side; the through-node path is closed and only updates `best`.

options: The tree could contain only negative values, so the answer can be negative
O(h) where h is tree height
